title: Boiler sales fell by a fifth — heat pumps took 7% of the market
excerpt: 1,450,900 domestic boilers and 110,353 heat pumps were sold into the UK market in 2025. Boilers still outsell heat pumps 13 to 1.
body: The UK sold 1,450,900 domestic boilers in 2025 — down from 1,886,100 in 2021 — while heat pump sales more than doubled over the same period, from 47,699 to 110,353 units. Heat pumps accounted for 7.1 per cent of boiler-plus-heat-pump sales, against 2.5 per cent four years earlier.

Both series are sales into the market rather than completed jobs. The boiler figures come from the European Heating Industry's annual Heating Market Reports; the heat pump figures are the Heat Pump Association's UK factory-gate sales, hydronic only, which exclude air-to-air units.

The distinction matters because the UK publishes three different heat pump counts for the same year, and they do not agree. For 2025: 110,353 sold into the market, 61,246 MCS-certified installations, and 53,265 retrofit installations in the DESNZ statistics. Each is correct on its own basis. There is no installation census for boilers at all, which is why sales are the only like-for-like comparison available.

Against the targets, the gap is the story. The Warm Homes Plan sets more than 450,000 heat pump installations a year by 2030, and the Climate Change Committee's pathway needs 158,587 retrofit installations in 2027. Retrofit installations in the first quarter of 2026 were 22 per cent lower than a year earlier.
sourceNote: Boilers: EHI Heating Market Reports 2023–2025. Heat pumps sold: Heat Pump Association UK (26 Mar 2026). Installations: MCS (Feb 2026) and DESNZ heat pump deployment statistics, official statistics in development (11 Jun 2026). Targets: DESNZ Warm Homes Plan (21 Jan 2026) and CCC 2026 progress report. Totals and shares are our own calculation from the published figures.

title: Siting rules relaxed — now the noise limit decides the job
excerpt: Permitted development finally allows the unit where it belongs. From 28 May 2026 an MCS 020(a) calculation at 37 dB(A) decides whether it stays permitted development.
body: Permitted development rights for air source heat pumps in England were substantially eased with effect from 29 May 2025. The one-metre boundary restriction is gone, the maximum outdoor unit size for houses rose from 0.6 m³ to 1.5 m³, detached houses may have up to two units, and air-to-air heat pumps are covered for the first time.

The condition that now governs the whole regime is noise. Since 28 May 2026, MCS 020(a) is the only accepted noise assessment in England: the installer must show by calculation that the predicted level does not exceed 37 dB(A) one metre from the nearest habitable-room window of a neighbouring property — tightened from the previous 42 dB(A).

The method matters as much as the number. MCS 020(a) works from the unit's sound POWER level rather than sound pressure and accounts for reflective surfaces and siting. Where the calculation cannot meet 37 dB(A), the job leaves permitted development and needs a full planning application.

In parallel, MCS itself has been through its biggest overhaul in two decades, rolling out across 2025 and 2026, with more weight on on-site quality and a six-year workmanship warranty. For specifiers the practical consequence is simple: sound power on the data sheet has become a planning variable, not a comfort footnote.
sourceNote: Rules as published for permitted development in England and MCS 020(a); planning decisions rest with the local authority. As of August 2026.

title: Boiler Upgrade Scheme rises to £9,000 for oil and LPG homes
excerpt: From 21 July 2026 the BUS pays up to £9,000 when off-gas-grid homes heated with oil or LPG switch to a heat pump.
body: From 21 July 2026 the Boiler Upgrade Scheme (BUS) offers a higher grant of £9,000 for a specific group of homes: properties not connected to the gas grid that currently heat with oil or LPG and switch to a heat pump. The standard £7,500 grant for air-to-water and ground-source heat pumps remains in place.
A new £2,500 support category for residential air-to-air heat pumps has also been added — a notable widening of the scheme beyond hydronic systems.

The policy signal matters as much as the number. The UK is turning its attention to the segment that is hardest to move: rural, off-gas-grid housing. These homes face volatile heating-oil prices and have strong heat pump potential, but the upfront installation cost has been the barrier — and £9,000 is aimed squarely at it.
For installers and manufacturers, the oil/LPG-to-heat-pump conversion market is becoming a segment in its own right, and one worth building offers around.
sourceNote: Figures as published for the Boiler Upgrade Scheme; eligibility is determined by the official bodies (DESNZ/Ofgem). As of July 2026.
